definition: Demean means to lower the dignity or status of someone.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word demean. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know demean should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The propeller cap and floppy shoes the theme park issues its PhD tour guides demean them a little more each summer.
A slight is far milder than demeaning treatment — one small, single omission, a skipped introduction or a name not remembered; to demean someone is to lower their standing steadily, day after day.
Humiliate goes further than demean — demeaning treatment wears dignity down; humiliation strips it off in front of an audience, all at once.

Degrade is the blunt twin of demean: it drags a person down hard and openly — shouted orders, public dressing-downs. To demean can be quiet, even polite-faced; the dignity is lowered by how someone is treated, with never a harsh word spoken.

An insult is one open blow — a slur, a sneer — that stings and passes. Demeaning treatment can smile the whole time: no single remark to point to, only an everyday arrangement that treats a person as smaller than they are.

Demean means to lower the dignity or status of someone.
The geriatric ward's training day begins with a clip: a nurse calling an eighty-year-old retired judge "sweetie pie" and asking whether "we" want "our" pudding.
Half the trainees laugh; the instructor waits them out.
The judge in the clip spent forty years being addressed as "Your Honor," she says, and baby talk strips it from him at the exact hour he cannot object.
Nothing in the voice is cruel.
Demean is the exact word for that baby talk, because it means to lower the dignity or status of someone — the harm lands on standing, not on feelings alone.
An insult stings and passes; demeaning treatment rearranges where a person ranks, and it can do so with a smile on.
Demean takes a person as its object; that is what separates it inside this crowded unit.
Debase lowers a thing's worth, denigrate blackens a name behind its back, deride laughs in its face — demean simply treats someone as smaller than they are, and can manage it politely.
Degrade is its blunter twin for harsher treatment.

The hospital's volunteer program was famous for recruiting retired surgeons, and infamous for what it did with them.
Okafor, who had run a trauma unit for thirty years, spent her first month directing visitors to the elevators and restocking the coffee cart.
No one was ever rude to her.
That was what made the arrangement demean her so effectively: every smiling shift assumed her judgment was worth nothing.
When she finally proposed a mentoring role for the retired staff, the coordinator looked genuinely surprised — then delighted.
The next season, volunteers were interviewed about what they knew, not just where they could stand.
